title: The VLT’s artificial star
caption: The laser guide star above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A pink haze fills the bottom of this frame, while the blues and whites of the Milky Way spread above. The blocky shapes in the foreground are the Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory, and a harsh yellow slash cuts right through the scene.

That streak is the VLT's laser guide star. It belongs to the telescope's adaptive optics system, which works to undo the blurring caused by the atmosphere. As light from space passes through the air, small local differences in the atmosphere distort it.

To correct for this, astronomers usually look for a bright star close to their target and use it as a reference. When no suitable star lies near enough, they make their own, shining a bright laser into the night sky to create an artificial one.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the pink haze and the Milky Way appear more vivid than they would to someone on the platform.

explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Gianluca Lombardi took the photograph under the dark skies above the Atacama, recording everything from the pink glow near the ground to the pale band of the Milky Way.
